sugarProductionAmericas.title: Sugar production in the Americas
sugarProductionAmericas.note: Rose from approximately 50,000 tonnes in 1700 to around 200,000 tonnes by the close of the American Revolution.

britishSugarImports.title: British sugar imports
britishSugarImports.note: Sevenfold increase 1700–1800. All monetary values in pounds sterling unless noted.

barbadosSugarShare.title: Sugar products share of Barbados total exports

jamaicaToBritain.title: Jamaica sugar exports destined for Britain
jamaicaToBritain.note: Between 1682 and 1701, Britain is the destination for more than 95% of Jamaica's sugar exports.

rawSugarBritishImports.title: Raw sugar share of all British imports, 1774
rawSugarBritishImports.note: Raw sugar accounts for one-fifth of all British imports, surpassing all other imported goods by a wide margin.

planterReceipts.title: Caribbean planters' gross receipts from sugar exports to Britain, 1713→1775
planterReceipts.note: Rose by a factor of 3.2, driven by rising demand in England and profitable re-export of refined sugar.

britishValueAdded.title: Total value added to the British economy by sugar production & trade
britishValueAdded.note: Captures surplus appropriated at each stage: cultivation, refining, re-export, final sale. £0.5m → £5.5m.

jamaicanSurplus.title: Surplus appropriated by Jamaican plantation owners, share of subsistence costs
jamaicanSurplus.note: Surplus extracted equals what is spent on subsistence of enslaved people by 1790.

muscovadoVsRefined.title: Price of refined sugar in England vs muscovado in Jamaica
muscovadoVsRefined.note: Fourfold difference 'completely out of proportion' to transport & refining cost → transfer pricing shifting profits to Britain.

colonyProfitability.title: Colonial vs 'mother country' investment profitability
colonyProfitability.note: Investments in the colonies are four to seven times more profitable than in England.

britishCapitalSlavery.title: British capital derived from enslaved-trade profits, 1770
britishCapitalSlavery.note: Stanley Engerman estimate: close to 40% of capital for Britain's commercial and industrial expansion.

britishNationalIncome.title: Combined enslaved-trade + sugar profits, share of British national income
britishNationalIncome.note: ~5%; underestimates total usurped profits; refining & re-export profits not added.

britishTransatlantic.title: British transatlantic slave trade, 1640–1807
britishTransatlantic.note: Portugal and Britain account for ~70% of all enslaved Africans transported to the Americas; centres Glasgow, Bristol, Manchester, London.

enslavedSeizedTotal.title: Total Africans seized for the transatlantic trade (incl. died in capture, marches, detention, Middle Passage)
enslavedSeizedTotal.note: At least 10 million landed in the Americas & Caribbean; plausibly 14–20 million seized in total. African population ~unchanged vs +300% in Asia & Europe 17th–19th c.

demographic.title: Population growth 17th–19th century
demographic.note: Asia & Europe grew 300%+; African population remained almost the same or declined; recovery only after abolition & independence.

jamaicaFactorConcentration.title: Jamaica arrivals, 28 Sep 1751 – 27 May 1752
jamaicaFactorConcentration.note: Seven thousand one hundred twenty-three enslaved Africans survived the Atlantic; delivered to nine factorage firms; three firms handle 83%.

hibbert.title: Thomas Hibbert, 'slave factor', 1764–1774
hibbert.note: Operation handled cargo for 61 ships & sale of 16,254 enslaved Africans; later co-founds Hibbert, Purrier & Horton (London).

jamaicaEnslavedPop.title: Enslaved population in Jamaica's five leading sugar parishes, 1720s→1788
jamaicaEnslavedPop.note: Increases more than sixfold; +206% in parishes ≥65% sugar vs +46% hinterland 1734–1788.

jamaicanWealth.title: Value of Jamaica's enslaved population, 18th century
jamaicanWealth.note: Avg ~£30/person; ~£25 million; closely matches Jamaica's total recorded wealth in 1774.

silverWorldShare.title: Spanish-American silver share of world supply, 1494–1850
silverWorldShare.note: Especially Mexico & Potosí (Bolivia); commodity money; ~real de a ocho.

musketExchange.title: Muskets exchanged per enslaved person
musketExchange.note: One enslaved person for two muskets early 1700s → at least fifteen by century's end; profits compensated rising prices.

barterTerms.title: Britain gross barter terms of trade with Africa (base 100, 1701–1750)
barterTerms.note: Increased 100→112 then sharply declined to 40 in 1800.

tariffs.title: Additional tariff to protect British refiners, after India became British colony
tariffs.note: High duties on refined sugar penalise colonial refining; low raw duties; +25% to block Indian sugar; 'not even a nail' in colonies.

gangSystem.title: Gang system structure
gangSystem.firstGang: young men & women late teens; most physical work 10–12 years
gangSystem.thirdGang: elderly + young children ('grass gang'); weeding & grass for animals
gangSystem.holesPerDay: 60–100 planting holes/day (2 cane plants each); 1.25 tonnes manure per acre
gangSystem.shifts: harvest season: 18–20h shifts, 6 days/week; engenho Sunday rules often unhonoured
gangSystem.mortality: two-fifths of newly arrived die within one year (Rev. Robert Robertson); 100% killed in 19 years (Edward Littleton, Barbados); higher mortality than cotton/coffee/tobacco

foundingTimes.title: Foundations predating the Industrial Revolution
foundingTimes.note: Dutch guilder (17th–18th c.) then British pound sterling; modern financial system rooted in genocide in the Americas, the enslaved trade & plantation system.
